study.title: Hosea 6 - Return to the LORD, to know his mercy and to reap what was sown
study.overview: The chapter presents a call to repentance in the midst of judgment. In the first verses, the people are invited to return to the LORD with hope of restoration; then God himself exposes the fragility of this response, because their faithfulness lasts little. Then the Lord states that he desires mercy and true knowledge, not just religious rites. The second half of the chapter shows how infidelity spread: there was transgression of the covenant, violence, priestly corruption and contamination of Israel. The outcome announces that Judah will also face harvest through its paths, although language allows different readings on whether this emphasizes judgment or restoration.

outline.title: Invitation around and hope of restoration
outline.explanation: The people are called to return to the Lord, acknowledging that he hurts for healing. The hope is that he relives and restores in the right time, and that the knowledge of God becomes a continuous movement, as certain as the dawn and the rains that make the earth fruitful.

outline.title: Human fidelity is brief, but God requires love and knowledge
outline.explanation: The Lord laments the instability of Ephraim and Judah: their goodness quickly disappears, such as fog or dew. The problem is not a lack of formal religion, but of a covenant lived with mercy and true knowledge of God, above sacrifices and burnt offerings.

outline.title: Generalized transgression and harvest for Judah
outline.explanation: The text describes the rupture of the covenant, violence in places and leaders, and impurity within Israel. Priests act as robbers, and even Judah is warned that there is also a prepared harvest when God brings back his people from misfortune.

study.context: The chapter moves in covenant language, as in a dispute of God with his people. The notes indicate that the call to repentance occurs in response to the acts of judgment of the LORD upon Israel, and that spring rains were important for the agricultural cycle. The religious scene is serious: leaders and priests appear as part of the problem, not as a solution. There are no additional historical details in the given notes other than this frame of sin, judgment and appeal around.
study.theology: Hosea 6 teaches that true repentance is not mere momentary emotion, but a real return to the Lord. God disciplines to heal, and his action has a restorative purpose. The chapter also highlights that the life of the covenant requires loyal love and personal knowledge of God, not only external sacrifices. Thus, religion without fidelity is empty. Sin is described as a breaking of the covenant and betrayal against God, and this unfaithfulness reaches both the people and their leaders. At the same time, the text maintains the tension between judgment and restoration: God corrects, denounces, and also calls the people to return.

scholarViews.insight: The first verses call the people to return to the Lord after their judgment, and the image of the spring rain shows the importance of restoration for the life of the earth.
The call "let us go back to the Lord," can be understood as mutual encouragement to repentance; the answer is to encourage others to seek God while there is conviction.

The expression "after two days" to the third day is seen by some as a possibility of reference to the death and resurrection of Christ, although Clarke presents it as an interpretation and not as absolute certainty.

questions: Is my faith expressed in lasting fidelity or only in passenger impulses, like morning fog?
Am I seeking to know God in a personal and obedient way, or just by fulfilling external religious practices?
What attitudes in my life show that I have sown for the flesh, and what kind of harvest can this produce?
study.practice: This week, practice a concrete return to the Lord: confess without excuse an area of infidelity, set aside time to seek God in prayer and reading, and demonstrate practical mercy to someone. Also examine whether their religious practices are accompanied by integrity, for the chapter insists that God wants loyalty and knowledge of him, not empty appearance.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow some readings, but do not close all questions. In 6:2, the possible relationship with the resurrection of Christ is presented by Adam Clarke as an interpretation, not as definitive proof of the text. In 6:11, the expression of Judah can be understood as an announcement of judgment, although Clarke also mentions the possibility of reading linked to the return of captivity. In addition, there are no more specific historical data in the notes beyond the general context of judgment, repentance and infidelity of the covenant.
